author: @HecioOliveira

text:
For the 1440p data with RT you kept saying that there was a CPU bottleneck and part of the time there wasn't.   You had to look ONLY at the RT data at 2K.  For instance GOTG 17:25 the RT Ultra data showed scaling going up the product stack so if it was CPU limited it was only the top end GPU, but this is a review of the 4080 not the 4090 and I'm betting more people will use it for 2K RT gaming than they will 4K RT gaming.

The issue with older GPUs vs. Lovelace is Lovelace is the first line of GPUs where you don't need to turn down quality settings, and to me this is important at this level of GPU, where the WHOLE POINT is quality graphics.  I mean that's what RT brings, high quality lighting effects that look more realistic.  So, testing these top end GPUs should now mean turning up the quality and running a game with RT enabled and ONLY using a tech like FSR or DLSS when you need to.  So to me the most important data was 2K, RT only, and 4K with DLSS, because that's how this GPU is most likely getting used.

In fact I don't even know why you included the RT off bars WHEN testing RT.  It didn't add anything.  You already showed that data and the only thing in my mind it added was confusion.  You only needed RT, RT + DLSS when testing RT.  THEN the graphs would have been more clear and you wouldn't have felt so compelled to say "CPU limited" when it really wasn't, for what you were testing, RT.

Not sure I agree with the Frame Generation conclusion, I'm afraid. 
FPS is ALWAYS all about perception, and not just a number telling how much it is. 
If Nvidias (and soon to be released FSR3) frame generation actually improves our perception, it is as good as native fps, as long as results goes. Sure, there are tons of glitches and IFs and BUTs, but the same could be said when DLSS and FSR first launched, and look where it is now. Mark my words: Frame generation will become one of the most important assets of a GPU in the next few years as the technology matures.

author: @unoriginalname771

text:
Half the point of increasing FPS, traditionally, was to reduce input latency.  DLSS 3, by contrast, is purely visual.  That doesn't mean DLSS 3 is useless or uninteresting or that it won't one day become important, but as a matter of principle, the extra frames generated by DLSS 3 must be differentiated from "regular" FPS.  The frames generated by DLSS 2.x will always be more useful.

The caveats built-in to DLSS 3's interpolation technology were well covered in Tim's video.  We will no doubt see the tech improved, but you can't get around certain limitations.  As Darude suggested, advancements in display panel tech will probably help DLSS 3 as much or more than anything else.  DLSS 3's relevance is inherently bound to refresh rates.  The main thing Nvidia needs to fix ATM is DLSS 3's incompatibility with V-Sync and FPS caps.
author: @RedundancyDept

text:
Beyond a certain point image smoothness stops to matter if input latency stays high. That's exactly what DLSS 3 offers. For looking at cutscenes it's potentially an improvement, for performing in gameplay best case scenario it's as good as DLSS 2.
Frame generation doesn't offer the feel of higher fps, merely the visuals, assuming the artifacts aren't distracting.

You're Romanian and are experiencing 13% year to year inflation rate. Multiply the introduction MSRP by 1.13. If the result is at or above the price of the cheapest 3080 you're not correct.

Comparing price levels to any given year in the past requires one to factor in inflation. Also note I simply took the year to year inflation rate, the inflation from September 2020 to 2021 isn't even factored in.

text: @1uponu705  Depends on the game but many times Ultra Shadows is the first that can be turned down. When going from "High" to "ULtra" in many games, all you are doing is increasing the resolution of a special effect which you really can't see well in gameplay. Simply increasing the resolution of something like a shadow by 25% can decrease performance by 5-10 fps without being able to see a difference. Forza Horizon 5 is a great example. Other things like Ambient Occlusion (High>Medium), Anti aliasing (at 4K aliasing isn't a big issue unless you're really close), Lens flares, depth of field, chromatic abberation, volumetric fog, etc. The only thing you never want to turn down is Texture Quality or Filtering (16x).  Again you should see if DIgital Foundry did a video on a game you're playing (Like FH5 or Cyberpunk) to see what they recommend for turning down.

@Piketom1  I really don't agree with any arguments you made for the 4080.  Yes it's a good card in a vacuum, but it doesn't exist in a vacuum and I can't think of any reason to get one over a 4090 at $1650 to $1700 (you can easily find in stock models at those prices).

"It's a very solid upgrade over the 3090 and allows you to really use a high end 4K display."

Yes it is, but that's for today's games.  It will certainly stay that way for a while, but if you're gaming on a 4K high refresh rate display, you're going to be getting a big advantage out of those extra CUDA cores and memory bandwidth of the 4090 before long.  Spending an extra $400-$500 today prevents you from having to buy a future $700+ GPU when games get more demanding (don't expect 4090 tier performance to get cheaper than that for many years).

Plus you have to consider the cost of the whole PC.  The 4090 may be 35%-40% more expensive, but probably only 15%-20% once you factor in the cost of the whole computer.  I also don't agree with the thermals and power argument.  If you're buying this tier of GPU, you should have no issues affording a case and PSU that can accommodate a 4090.  Plus the 4080 is still a 320W card, which is higher than anything the 20 series or earlier had.

You compare the 2080 Ti to the 4080, but the 2080 Ti was only able to cost $1200 because it was "the best."  If there was a card that was 30% faster for 33% more money for the Turing generation, everyone would've said to buy that instead.

To be clear, if I were building a PC today I would build it around the 6700 XT or a used ~6800 XT/3080 12GB tier card depending on used prices for the latter (say $350 for 6700 XT, ~$600 for the other two).  But looking at 4080 vs 4090, there's no situation where buying the 4080 makes sense outside of a substantial price drop.

It will last a lot longer at that resolution. You will not be CPU limited with a ryzen 3000 or 5000 series CPU (4000 is just 3000 with iGPU) in most games. It can even do RTX at 1440p with DLSS quality even in Cyberpunk (I had a 3080 with 5800X for 2 years).
